Today, Switzerland is a bilingual country, as well as Belgium and Luxemburg; there are African and South American nations where the people speak fluently their mother tongue and French or English, and sometimes three languages.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Again, several countries are a proof that bilingualism can exist even if it sometimes gives rise to certain inevitable wrangles. As quarrels sometimes arise between members of the same family, so can they happen sometimes, as to details, between members of a bilingual nation. But as concerns the essential, people understand themselves better when they can speak in languages they usually understand, and when they do not need interpreters to be understood.

After all, Mr. Speaker, what is it we want in this country? If an English-speaking Canadian can speak French, apart from the personal prestige this will give him, the pleasure of being more easily on friendly terms with his fellow-citizens, of being more efficient, he will be able to count on his government's gratitude if he works in the public service. As for the French Canadian who has made the effort of learning English, he will benefit from the same advantages.
The purpose is also to make French Canadians feel at home throughout the country, as English Canadians feel at home when they come to Quebec, because their language is spoken there, first as a gesture of courtesy and also for the sake of brotherhood between fellow-citizens of a same country.
Again, nobody will be forced to know both languages at once. It is merely a matter of prompting all those who can do it to do so and also of asking that public service officials deal with all Canadians in one or another of the official languages.
The fact will obviously remain that apart from professional efficiency, people able to speak two, three or even four languages will always be more qualified and superior, all things being equal, to others. To those who understand that, I would suggest that they learn three or four.
Still, this is a field, Mr. Speaker, which can lead to anger, sentimentality, stirring of popular passions, demagoguery, fanaticism or jingoism-it could easily be done-because one's mother tongue is something fundamental to the human being. It enables him to express his innermost feelings. I have seen several cases such as that. I have seen many cases of it back home. I still see some occasionally but I do believe I see more cases of it elsewhere in Canada when persuing its history in the last few years.
I am appealing to our English-speaking brothers elsewhere in Canada who are sensible, that an end be put to the exaggerations of recent years of our angry young men in Quebec, because they are fed up with injustices, with promises that never come to anything.
Once again, I appeal to the conscience of all the members. I urge them not to listen to the complaints of those who in fact indulge in this type of discrimination and who will not, or cannot, understand that there really can be two peoples who are both entitled to their own mother tongue.
May 20, 1969

I feel it behooves each and every member to go back home and explain that principle to those of their constituents who And it difficult to understand, and to show them that Quebec is not asking for favours but, as the hon. member for Charlevoix said this afternoon, merely to be treated as all the other citizens are across Canada, as we were treated with fairness. .. .so far, when it was a question of paying taxes or of serving in the army to save the fatherland.
Mr. Chairman, corporations realize these things today; and they offer courses to their employees.
A constitutional argument is put forward. They are trying to be legalistic in order to oppose this decision of parliament which will entrench once and for all what we have been waiting for over a century. However, it is not a question that will be solved simply by raising constitutional objections because there are six millions Canadians who feel in their hearts and souls that time has come for them to be put on an equal footing with everybody else.
Out of this number, more than five millions in my province will no longer accept, tomorrow, to be treated as inferior beings. They were requested, in order to be allowed to work in the public service, to speak English. They learned it, even when they did not need it. We ask our English-speaking fellow-citizens to do the same thing towards the French-Canadians.
It is possible to add fuel to the fire, but I think that in conclusion I could do no better than to thank and to congratulate all the members who have acknowledged this principle.
In particular, I congratulate the leader of my party, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who had the courage to bring in the bill.
I thank and I commend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Douglas) as well, for approving the guiding principle of the bill. I also thank the leader of the Rallie-ment Creditiste (Mr.. Caouette) for defending that cause.
We may have different opinions on how to implement the bill, but I think that if, as a matter of principle, we favour demogoguent and discrimination, if we are divided instead of being united and trying to persuade all Canadians that this an important and urgent matter, we shall have done a disservice to this country.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is too important to allow such an attitude. That is why I am happy to see that many of my colleagues of all parties approve the principle of this bill, which will make the next century a more prosperous one, because Canadians will understand each other better. Instead of creating confusion in their relations, they will speak languages they will understand.
I conclude by recalling a few words from Saint-Exupery, and I quote:
The greatest vocation for men is to unite men-
-and the best way to unite them is to help them speak languages they all understand.

Mr. Speaker, under the new rules of procedure in the house, at this stage we are making suggestions preliminary to the submission of the legislation to the special committee that will be set up to deal further with this matter. Ordinarily, there would not be an extended debate at this period. However, I shall take this opportunity afforded by second reading to make recommendations which I trust will be taken into consideration by the committee when it begins to focus on this bill. I do so at this stage because, from rather bitter experience, I am discovering that the new procedures have a tendency to make it extremely difficult for a private member of the House of Commons to have direct participation in discussion at the committee stage.
We have only a few members of the house represented on the committee. I recall the recent debate on Bill C-150. It was impossible, following the consideration of the matter at the committee stage, for a private member to have amendments to the bill taken seriously into consideration. Again this afternoon we ran into a further complication arising from the committee system. The Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, which is concerned with matters pertaining to the department of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), was called together to sit while the house was sitting. Some of us raised a protest in the committee this afternoon and pointed out that there was another extremely important matter under consideration in the House of Commons. I think all hon. members will agree that the House of Commons has first call upon the services of members of parliament, including the members of the executive. It was doubly important that members of this committee should be in the house, because the

Secretary of State is piloting this legislation through the house.
As a result of attendance at the committee I was, unfortunately, unable to hear the statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) whom we thought would be responsible for dealing with this important issue in the house. Therefore, the comments I shall make this evening will be without the benefit of having heard his speech. The attention of several hon. members of the house was divided due to what I thought was the unnecessary calling together of the Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts to deal with another matter, that of putting Telesat into orbit. It is very difficult to understand why at this stage the government is putting pressure on hon. members to deal with other matters, particularly when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Secretary of State and other hon. members have pointed out that Bill C-120 is considered of most urgent importance, inasmuch as it is concerned with the preservation of national unity in this country.

speechtext:
As I explained in the committee, and this is one of the problems with our committee system which is destroying the effectiveness of this House of Commons, I was busily engaged in the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It is impossible to be in two places at once. But the point I am making here, which seems to be irritating the hon. gentleman opposite, is that the government is downgrading the role of parliament, and this has been the case in respect of this bill. It was introduced before we actually knew its final form. Some amendments have been placed before us, but they have no significance at all until they are put before the committee and a decision is made on whether or not the committee approves them. Opposition members have not even had the opportunity to propose amendments, so it is in a sort of never-never atmosphere that we are debating this important subject at the moment. I think it was Mr. Charles Lynch, in an article following the debate on Friday, who said that it was an act of lunacy on the part of the government to irritate parliament on a controversial matter of this nature by failing to put the amendments before the house.
I enjoyed the statement made by the Secretary of State when he introduced the bill. He speaks English with an accent that would have charmed the heart of my old Irish mother, and he speaks it in a way that indicates he has already assumed the mantle of the
May 20, 1969

minister of culture. Of course, the ministry of culture, when and if it is established in Canada, would require all the arts of the propagandist. I thought that the Secretary of State on Friday afternoon handled his assignment very effectively from that standpoint. But the truth of the matter is-and this is proof of the fact that the government is schizophrenic and of two minds on these matters-the government was emphasizing in the committee the fact that Telestat and other developmental programs that are concerned with the economy of Canada are the real stuff and substance of national progress and development. I am speaking tonight as one who has strongly supported the notion that the government priorities at this stage in the parliamentary session should be in the direction of economic matters rather than symbolic or cultural matters. This opinion is supported by some very sound leaders from the province of Quebec as well as from other provinces of Canada.
I speak tonight as a representative of a western constituency, a part of Canada that is faced with a problem of extreme economic consequence if it is not dealt with very quickly by this dilatory government. I am referring of course to the problem of the grain situation on the prairies. Ever since parliament came together last fall, western members have been asking the government for emergency action to deal with the crisis among the grain growers of the prairies which is becoming more acute with each passing day. All we get in response is the lethargic attitude of the government that in due course they will do something about this matter. Obviously, they do not understand the economy of the prairies because the farmer is into another crop year. He is faced with indebtedness from the past year because he cannot pay his debts until he sells his crop. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart) this afternoon, a good many shipping points in the west are still on the unit basis. They do not even have their initial quotas.
I want to protest in the strongest terms against this failure of the government of the just society to come to grips with the real issues that are gnawing at the vitals of national unity and of the Canadian confederation. I have good support for this stand from within the cabinet ranks and I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) will deal with this matter in the House of Commons because, in a strongly worded speech to the provincial Liberal leadership convention a week ago Saturday in the city of

I would like to point out also that in the past the problems of confederation and national unity that have torn the body politic asunder have not been related to cultural, social or linguistic issues but rather economic discontent.

speechtext:
Speaking to the point of order for the moment, Mr. Speaker. I would have thought the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) would have shared the opinion of his colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) that economic issues are just as important as these other questions, if not more so, when it comes to solving the problems of the Canadian body politic. I think that what I am saying has to be said by the western members. I trust the hon. member for St. Boniface will join with us and with his hon. friend the Minister of Supply and Services, in repeating here in the House of Commons what the latter had to say in Winnipeg last week.
Economic problems are always reflected in social and political issues. I have already intimated that the progressive movement was a reflection of economic conditions in agrarian Canada. It is trite to say that Canada is a difficult nation to govern. Our friends of the just society government are finding this out. Problems do not wither away in the aura of charisma; one has to deal with continuing economic reality.
In his speech the other day the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) said that unity does not demand uniformity. We all agree with that statement. Others have said you can only get unity out of diversity in Canada. It has required great quantities of goodwill and tolerance to achieve the splendid degree of national unity from sea to sea which has been realized in Canada out of such diverse ethnic groups. It always amazes me when I travel to different parts of Canada to see the way in which we have been able to continue as a nation, and to progress as a nation, while at the same time permitting the various ethnic groups which make up Canada to retain their language and certain aspects of their culture-in western Canada, even certain linguistic rights.
I do not think western Canada has to apolo-pize to anybody, including the Secretary of State,, with regard to the progress which has been made in recent years toward the acceptance of what is commonly known these days as the French fact. The province of Manitoba has offered leadership in this respect under
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
the Hon. Duff Roblin when he was premier. There was no coercion; this was based on a spirit of goodwill and tolerance which is the essence of the mosaic concept so widely held in Manitoba.
In recent years, unfortunately, Canada, which used to be a shining example to the world of the virtues of tolerance, goodwill and mutual respect for ethnic, cultural and linguistic differences has begun to sound somewhat like a banana republic rather than the true north, strong and free. This relates to what is sometimes called the quiet revolution-actually, it has not been very quiet. It has created an atmosphere of uncertainty and disequilibrium which has made it difficult for many parts of Canada to continue along the pathway to nationhood which had become established as a way of life.
I have some relevant quotations here but time will not permit me to read them. Serious commentators have pointed out that what is really disturbing the balance of national unity in Canada is the export of the quiet revolution. As that quiet revolution is exported it tends to become more noisy, with the consequent debates which have been rocking the Canadian body politic in recent years.
Canada is a nation of minorities. We talk about the English speaking majority but in terms of population this majority is made up of many minorities most of which, in western Canada, still retain their ethnic ways of life. I do not need to belabour this point. In my own province, as in each of the prairie provinces, there are islands of cultural identification which are quite distinct. These people conduct their church services in their own languages, even broadcast in their own languages; this is something which is difficult, perhaps, for other hon. members who come from other parts of Canada to appreciate, but it does belie statements made by some people to the effect that the west is intolerant, that it wants to go back to the Plains of Abraham, and all that other nonsense. We are trying to get away from all that narrow nationalistic nonsense which tore up Europe and which was, in fact, the reason so many of those who belong to these ethnic groups came to Canada in the first place. They had suffered too much in the wars and quarrels of the 19th century and they came to Canada because it was a shining example of goodwill and tolerance toward ethnic and cultural differences.
It is not hard to stir up trouble in Canada because of the variety of ethnic minorities which exist. We like to say we are all equal, although I suppose it is possible to add that
May 20, 1969

some are more equal than others. We talk of founding races. For myself, I do not like this phrase; it sounds too much like the racism of Germany before the second world war, the kind of propaganda which Dr. Goebbels, minister of culture of nazi Germany, used to try to get across to the people having to do with pan-Germanism and all that nonsense which tore Europe asunder in the most bloody holocaust the world has ever seen.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I often wonder what our Indian friends who, after all, were here long before any of us, think of this. As one of them said humorously, if the Indians had had more restrictive immigration laws perhaps Canada would not be facing the trouble it faces at present.
Progress has been made through gradual development. It is always encouraging to see the children of immigrants, the second generation Canadians, proudly declare their unhyphenated Canadianism. Unfortunately, as I say, there is trouble in Canada at the present time and parliament will have to deal with it in the next few weeks. Why is there trouble, particularly in western Canada? I think the nub of the matter is that this legislation represents compulsion to many, and no one likes legislative compulsion. The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) had this to say to the Social Credit League of Manitoba recently, as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune of April 19:
I'm against that kind of an act, because it implies compulsion and I'm strongly opposed to government compulsion.
If passed, the act would guarantee French in the federal civil service, the courts, and schools in areas throughout Canada where there is a large French population.
Then he spoke about the point I was referring to a few minutes ago. The newspaper report reads as follows:
The problem of the wheat farmer is worse, as far as Canada's economy is concerned-much more than the language question. Mr. Trudeau's fault was that he gave the impression everyone ... would have to learn French, said Mr. Caouette.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is the compulsory aspect of legislative prescriptions that disturbs all the folk who have come to Canada to escape the sort of thing that has bedogged pre-war and post-war Europe and that has produced the worst global wars of history.
Some have said that the bill is unnecessary and all that is necessary is for us to carry out the spirit of the British North America Act. I
Official Languages
agree. The spirit of the British North America Act has been moving forward with amazing speed in recent years, as seen by the application of broadcasting principles and the introduction of simultaneous translations in the House of Commons. When I was first a member of Parliament eighteen years ago, French was rarely heard here. Only those hon. members coming from Quebec, certain parts of northern Ontario and New Brunswick were truly bilingual. I studied French all through college and I am still not bilingual. It is not a living language for me because I have not been exposed to it and have not had to work with it. It has not become the language of my everyday life, and here lies the problem with legislative compulsion. The government realizes this, and that is why it has introduced amendments. The government has heard complaints from the prairies and from its own supporters. It is introducing these amendments to try to sweeten the semblance of legislative compulsion inherent in the bill, and thus make the bill more acceptable to its own supporters as well as to the people of Canada. Whether the amendments will do this we do not know. In any event, those amendments must be produced in the committee.
The constitutional question has been raised. I referred to it in passing. Many say this legislation is unnecessary; that it is a bit of window dressing and that it will give power to some. Perhaps this bill is the basis for the ministry of culture that the Secretary of State wishes to set up. As he has said many times across Canada, once this legislation has been passed he will have the tools in his hand with which to operate a ministry of culture and impose the views that he wishes to get across to us. As the Leader of the Opposition said, the committee will have to consider very carefully the constitutional question. The question of provincial rights is of great concern to the premiers of western Canada.
The Prime Minister blows hot and cold on this issue. Recently he had a quarrel with the former Minister of Transport on the interpretation of federalism. The former Minister of Transport says that he is a federalist, whereas the Prime Minister is a provincial rightist. That is an internal, family quarrel about which we have no exact information. I hope the Prime Minister will take part in this debate, because it is most important for him to do so. It seems that on this question the Prime Minister is espousing the other side of the coin. He seems to uphold the right of Ottawa to interfere in the cultural affairs of each of our provinces.

May 20, 1969
Official Languages
The bilingual district issue has been raised. Bilingual districts obviously will lead to ghettos which will engender problems similar to those of Indian reservations. Segregation of people always creates cultural ghettos. This issue has raised a strong reaction from the other western ethnic groups. "What about us" they say. When the Prime Minister campaigned in the west they asked him, "will we have the privilege of establishing linguistic districts or bilingual districts," and the Prime Minister said, "yes, if there is a request for that." Mr. Speaker, that answer only confused the situation. You cannot have cultural purity in the sort of world we live in and you cannot keep your linguistic purity. For instance, it is said that Americans, and particularly those of the United States, no longer speak English; that the language they speak has now become completely transformed. If a person from the southern United States speaks to someone from the northern half of the continent it is said an interpreter is needed to bridge the gulf between the two kinds of English spoken. Adulteration of a language takes place very rapidly, and we see that happening in western Canada where a new Canadianism, distinct from anything that has existed hitherto, is being created. It is rising rapidly and is based, as I have indicated, on the goodwill and tolerance generated by those who live in our western Canadian mosaic.
In its present form this measure is divisive. The Prime Minister understands this, and that is why he is trying to bring in amendments. The Minister of Justice also understands this. He travelled across the country trying to soften the divisive impact of the legislation. The Secretary of State has travelled across the country, too, but his statements have aggravated the situation. I do not think he realizes what the effect of some of his statements in western Canada has been. I will mention one or two of those statements, then perhaps he will understand why so much concern was expressed in western Canada following his pilgrimages there. In his speech before the founding meeting of the Societe Franco-Manitobaine in St. Boniface, he forecast the placement of federal inspectors or control officers across the country to promote bilingualism in the designated bilingual districts. They would be sort of "gauleiters" for bilingualism in the west.

Remember, Mr. Speaker, I interpret this measure as an attempt to assure that each and every citizen can communicate or deal with the federal government in either of the two official languages. It does not, as I see it, compel English speaking Canadians to speak French. Nor, on the other hand, does it compel French speaking Canadians to speak English. I rely, and I certainly hope the rest of this country, can as well on the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he addressed the last federal-provincial conference. His statement on this matter is so very important I think perhaps it should be read into the record of this house, then if any misinterpretation arises at a later date we can refer to it. This is what he said when he spoke to the last federal-provincial conference:
Our policy of bilingualism has been widely misunderstood. It does not mean that every English speaking Canadian must learn to speak French any more than it means that every French speaking Canadian must learn to speak English. It means that every Canadian will have access to public education in either official language and will be free to use either language in dealing with the federal government and other public bodies in all areas of the country where the size of the minority justifies it.
I hope I am not naive enough to believe that the Prime Minister of this country would make that statement at such an important meeting as a federal-provincial conference, to all the premiers of this country, unless he really believed that to be the purpose behind the bill. I suggest the bill itself does not impose bilingualism on the people of this country, but rather attempts to insure that all Canadians irrespective of where they live will feel equally at home.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) also made a very important observation during the same federal-provincial conference which I feel should be read into the record of this house for future reference. This is what the Minister of Justice said:
This is not a bill to force compulsory bilingualism on the citizens of Canada. This is a bill enabling the citizens of Canada where they are found in sufficient numbers to approach the facilities of the federal government in either the French or the English language.

I suggest in all seriousness that there is nothing the matter with that objective. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principle of the bill and its real thrust is stated at the very outset in the clause which declares the status of languages. That clause reads:
The English and French languages are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the parliament and government of Canada, and possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the parliament and government of Canada.
This principle seems so appropriate, so logical and so inevitable for our country that looking back from the vantage point of 1969 it seems rather surprising that we did not have its provisions written into our constitution in 1867. Perhaps, indeed, the Fathers of Confederation were closer to this principle than we now realize, because if we look at the federal act of 1870 which established the government of Manitoba we find that the same linguistic guarantee which occurs in section 133 of the British North America Act is found in section 23 of that act. If we had continued to have what is perhaps the early spirit of confederation, along with the good will which seems natural to it, we would probably not have had the school question in Manitoba, regulation 17 in Ontario, or the innumerable slights, too small for history to record but too large for memory to forget, which have marked the experience of many French speaking citizens in various provinces of this country. But we now have a second opportunity, a second chance, and the wit and resolution to take advantage of it. It is to be hoped that this measure we are debating tonight will be soon supplemented by provincial action and ultimately by constitutional amendment.
Official Languages
The principal legal arguments against the bill are without either substance or shadow of merit. The argument based on section 91 (1) of the B.N.A. Act is to the effect that that section denies to parliament any power to legislate respecting the use of the English or French languages. But the fact is that section 91 (1) merely prohibits the amendment of section 133 to prevent any derogation from the limited constitutional rights granted in that section respecting the use of the languages. The official languages bill does not in any way derogate from the guarantees contained in section 133, and therefore does not offend section 91 (1).
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The second argument is based on an interpretation of section 133 as a limitation on the use of the French language rather than as a guarantee of the minimum use of that language. The fallacy of this interpretation is obvious from the fact that section 133 refers equally to the English and French languages. The limitation in section 133 is thus clearly for a minimum and not a maximum of usage.
The third legal argument is to the effect that the coincidence of what is proposed in Bill C-120 with constitutional changes proposed by the federal government shows that this is a matter for which a constitutional amendment is necessary. But even if there were an identity of content, the argument would be a non sequitur. What constitutional enshrinement would add would be a limitation on federal power henceforth to repeal the law which by ordinary federal standards of statute making would be repealable.
As a simple example may I point out that I assume many hon. members join with me in feeling that even if we are not able to get a bill of rights in the near future which may, among other things, prohibit the introduction of illegally obtained evidence in the court room, we should go ahead and insert a provision in the Criminal Code to prevent the introduction of such evidence even in the absence of a constitutional provision. There may be a coincidence of the two provisions, but this does not prevent legislation in advance of constitutional amendments.
It is true that there is no explicit power with regard to language in the British North America Act for either level of government. This means that it either comes under the federal residual power or-and this is the more usual interpretation-it is ancillary to other powers in the constitution. The federal government therefore can legislate with

May 20, 1969
Official Languages
regard to language only in areas of federal jurisdiction, federal government institutions, and areas of federal authority such as procedure in the criminal courts.
It seems to me that the only legal argument which presents some difficulty is that which gets us into the rather murky divide between criminal procedure, which is a federal power under subsection 27 of section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, and the constitution of courts of criminal jurisdiction, which is part of the administration of justice and a provincial power under section 92(14) of the B.N.A. Act. This situation is even more confused because of the procedural jurisdiction which the federal government has allowed the provinces to exercise over the years even though constitutionally the power was in the hands of the federal government. But except with regard to this point, the force of which has now been largely removed by the amendment which the government proposes to introduce, and on which therefore I will not dwell, the legal case against the official languages bill does not, in my opinion, rise to the level of intellectual respectability.
What is important is not that the legal arguments are bad but that they are raised at all. This shows the concern among many of our fellow citizens about the effect of this legislation. To the extent that such concern arises from a rejection of the symbolic nature of the change which we hope to bring about by virtue of this act, it seems to me that we can neither accept it nor compromise with it. Both historically and functionally this country has a bilingual character.
I would not want this to be confused with biculturalism. Our country is, and I hope will remain, a multi-cultural country in which many cultures which have come from other parts of the world continue to exist and enrich the Canadian mosaic to which we sometimes refer. Our country is multi-cultural but it is also bilingual. The symbol of bilingualism must be maintained. The fact of biculturalism must also be maintained.
But to the extent that the concern about this bill expresses the fear of discrimination against people themselves and their families, especially with regard to employment, there is something I believe, that we must take into account.
My own riding of Windsor-Walkerville is one in which all the currents of the country at present are felt. We will have the privilege of being part of the bilingual district which I expect, on the recommendation of the Royal 
Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, Essex county will become. We have a very large ethnic population and we also have a heavy concentration of industrial employees. These last two groups are among those which in our country have subjectively real fears, that some aspects of this bill, or rather some possible means of carrying it out, might restrict their opportunities in our country. I believe we must see to it that these subjectively real fears do not become objectively real and valid as the act begins to be applied.
The official who will enforce this act has been referred to as a linguistic ombudsman. I believe he will have the duty of seeing to it, not only that the rights of French speaking peoples in various parts of the country are protected, but also that in the creation of new rights for the French speaking minority the opportunities of other groups in the country whose native language is neither English nor French are not subjected to unduly restrictive pressures. The linguistic ombudsman will have a job to do on both sides.
We share a continent with an economically powerful and culturally aggressive neighbour. I say to some of my friends opposite who are troubled about this bill and yet are very concerned with the importance of maintaining our separation from the United States, that there is no surer guarantee of our retaining our independence than through the institution of official bilingualism in this country. It is historically true that our French speaking compatriots in large part saved us from being submerged in the United States both at the time of the revolutionary war and during the war of 1812 to 1814. But the argument in favour of bilingualism is not such a negative one-it is a positive one. It creates an opportunity, not only for our French speaking citizens, but for all of us, to share in a cultural life which is richer by reason of being linguistically fuller.
There is no compulsion in this bill except on the federal government. There is no compulsion on the citizens of this country to learn or speak French. The only compulsion is on the government. For the people, there is freedom.

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, April 23, as recorded in Hansard at page 7859, after there had been a reference to the budget or the budget speech which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said he would be making toward the end of May or in the early part of June, I put the following question to the minister:
In preparing his budgetary statement, is the minister still considering including in it a provision so that taxation will not continue to be levied on old age pensioners who have only their pensions and the guaranteed income supplement on which to live?
The reply of the Minister of Finance was in these words:
In the preparation of the budget we consider all submissions which have been made to the government in this regard.
That was about the fourth or fifth time that the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary secretary had assured the house concerning the question of making necessary adjustments so that those who have only the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement will not have to pay income tax on that income. The matter was discussed in the late show on April 1 as well as on March 5 and on one or two other occasions. There have been a number of questions on the orders of the day, and it came into the debate on March 17 when we spent a full day on the question of pensions.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I want to say quite frankly that I have been around here long enough to know that budget secrets are not given out in advance. But I have also been around here long enough to know that there are certain things which have to be pressed for repeatedly, desirable though they may be, before the government can be induced to act as it should. I plead very strongly that whatever else the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) may do in his May or June budget he will deal with this matter, because I am sure all of us in the house think it is most unfair for

Nevertheless, it seems to me that this is a situation which nobody intended. I do not blame the government for it happening in the first place, but I do blame the government for not doing something about it.
The present income tax exemption levels were set in 1949. They are due for a change, there is no question about that. But in 1949 the old age pension was much lower. Speaking of technicalities, I was quite interested in a sentence used by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce on Friday of last week. The occasion was the discussion during the oral question period of the $80 million which the government forgave to the automobile industry. This is a case of $80 million which should have been paid, according to the law, by the automobile manufacturers, but it was forgiven by order in council. Be this as it may, when the matter was the subject of questions and answers on Friday of last week, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said this: "This is why we have been quite willing to accommodate the industry when some technicalities arose. This is what we have done in the remission of $80 million in potential tariff which the government of Canada could have collected under an agreement."

COMMUNICATION-BELL CANADA-ALLEGED DISREGARD OE INVESTMENT RETURN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 1 I asked the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) whether he, on behalf of the government, would make representations to the Canadian Transport Commission in order to oppose the request of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada to increase its profit to 9 per cent on invested capital. This is not the first such request on the part of Bell of Canada. On a number of occasions that company has asked for its rates to be increased. It has wished for higher profits but has consistently ignored orders issued by government regulatory agencies. During the 1950's the regulatory agency of the day, Board of Transport Commissioners, fixed Bell's return in a judgment at $2.43 per share. In 1964 this rate was equivalent to a 5.9 per cent profit on Bell's over-all capital.
Despite that order of the board limiting Bell's profit to $2.43 per share, Bell earned substantially more than that in 1959 and every year following. In 1959 the company made $2.48 per share; in 1960 profits were $2.52 per share; in 1961 they were $2.50; in 1962 they were $2.66; in 1963 they were $2.58; in 1964 they were $2.71 and in 1967 they reported a return of 6.8 per cent on invested capital. At that time the Board of Transport Commissioners, in a ruling handed down, had allowed the company a return of about 6.6 per cent on invested capital.
Despite its earlier order, the Board of Transport Commissioners in January, 1968,
May 20, 1969	COMMONS
decided that Bell could maintain a 6.8 per cent return without reducing its telephone rates. For the year ending March 31, 1969, Bell's return on invested capital was 7 per cent. Yet the Board had set a legal limit on profits of 6.8 per cent. Not satisfied with twice violating the orders of the Board regulating their rate structure, Bell Canada now has the gall to apply for permission to increase telephone rates so they can make a return of 9 per cent on their invested capital. The ability of Bell to ignore orders of the regulatory agency is a serious matter to the people of Ontario and Quebec. The minister, as a member of parliament from Quebec, certainly realizes that a profit increase of J per cent to 1 per cent for Bell Telephone represents an overpayment by the people of Ontario and Quebec of between $10 million and $20 million a year.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In a similar situation a few years ago in the State of California, the public utilities commission of that state ordered a refund to the telephone subscribers of $60 million because they found that the Telephone Company of California had overcharged the subscribers by that amount. I suggest the government of Canada insist that the regulatory agency enforces its rules. The government has the staff,, economists and statisticians, necessary to examine the whole problem of rate structure and profits of Bell Canada. I suggest they make recommendations to the regulatory agency, the Canadian Transport Commission, along these lines.

REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-ATLANTIC DEVELOPMENT BOARD-GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 8 I asked a question concerning the third report of the Atlantic Development Board on fisheries. I must admit that I am in favour of most parts of this report, but the portion that concerns me greatest is the idea of concentrating operations in a single port. I am wondering how you can take a viable, established fishing industry and suggest that it be dismantled in favour of other parts of the country.
How can we suggest to a fisherman or farmer, as other reports have done, that he must move to another part of the country? What we are really telling him is to sell his gear and equipment and move to the city. I am not against the Atlantic Development Board. It has done a tremendous job, but I am concerned about this whole idea of centralization. I suggest there is a lack of planning, particularly on the part of government, with respect to the way we are presently going. The present trend is to centralization, to get rid of our countryside and to urbanize everything. But what will happen in 20 years time? In 20 or 25 years time we shall have to think of moving the people back to the country, and of getting them away from the city. I suggest that the computers have not calculated far enough ahead.
May 20, 1969
8882	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I object to the idea of certain growth centres being built up at the expense of rural Canada. For example, I can think of Halifax and Saint John in Atlantic Canada. I do not mind these centres being developed at the expense of Montreal or Toronto, but I object very strongly if they are to be developed at the expense of the countryside surrounding them. The people living in rural Canada are slowly being deprived of the necessary facilities and services. In this connection I am thinking of post offices, customs houses and other facilities. If taking away these things is the answer to our problems, then again I object very strongly.
What is happening in our fishing communities? Post offices are being closed. Wharves are being allowed to deteriorate. Fish are being taken by foreign vessels, thus reducing markets for our own fishermen. Fishing communities do not need much to survive and survive well. They require that their wharves be maintained, that dredging take place in some places, and that lighthouses and coast guard facilities be provided. These are the basic and simple things required for the proper management of the fishing industry. Once these services deteriorate then one has no choice but to think of centralization, and this has been happening within the past couple of years.
I know of one company in my area whose manager told me last week that if something is not done soon he will have to move out and go to another part of the country. Industry is viable in the southwestern part of Nova Scotia, as in many other parts of Canada. At least the present industries there are viable. One need only look at the statistics to see this. We find an increase in the number of boats, and in the catch in all parts of southwestern Nova Scotia. Why should we want to concentrate all this into one single port?
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
We might look at the statistics in respect of Yarmouth, Digby, Pubmico and Cape Sable

Island. I received a brief last week from the Clare Board of Trade. It shows that in 1950 the approximate value of boats owned by fishermen was $350,000. Now, it is over $5 million. The landed value of the catch in 1950 was around $389,000. Now this has increased to $2 million or almost $3 million. The number of fishermen employed has increased greatly.
This is the reason I am concerned about any report or any thought of too much centralization. I hope the government can base its policies and decisions on facts and weigh these facts against the present tendencies. Last week I expressed concern outside the house and I repeat that the cities are getting richer and rural Canada is getting poorer. We must at least provide the basic facilities.

The minister considers the reports of the Atlantic Development Board to be important and valuable studies. He was, therefore, very glad to act on the board's request that they should be published even though most of the texts are reaching their final stage only since the board in its previous form was replaced by the Atlantic Development Council.
The minister and his officials will certainly be paying close attention to these studies in their formulation, in consultation with the provinces, of plans and programs for economic expansion in the Atlantic region. The factual and analytical material in the studies will, indeed, be essential to the work of the new department.
Recommendations made in the reports will also be carefully considered, but of course it should be understood that the publication of the reports in no way means that the views expressed are necessarily those of the minister. The recommendations will be considered along with others.
